topic.title: the third partner
topic.claim: In urban dual-income homes, the house help is the reason the marriage looks equal; her day off shows who really runs the house.

paragraphs: In most urban Indian homes, the marriage has a third partner.
She arrives at 8 and leaves by 11.
Both of you work. Both of you are tired. You split the rent, the EMI, the Netflix.
And the house runs so smoothly that nobody ever has to ask who does what.
Then one morning, the WhatsApp arrives.
"Didi, aaj nahi aaungi."
By 9 AM, the most honest audit of your marriage has begun.
Who does the dishes. Who sweeps. Who remembers the dusting nobody ever noticed she did.
And the audit usually reaches the same finding: the work doesn't split down the middle. It slides back to the wife.
India's own time-use survey says the same: women who do housework spend about five hours a day on it. Men, about an hour and a half.
Here's what nobody says out loud. Urban India never settled who does the housework.
It outsourced the question, for ₹10,000 a month, and called the answer equality.
That money buys back two, maybe three hours a day for the woman of the house.
It's probably the best-returning money the family spends. Nobody budgets it that way.
And the didi who sent that message has a home too.
Her own dishes, her own kids' tiffin, packed at 6 AM before she gets to yours. The equality you paid for ends at her doorstep.
So when that message comes, don't treat it as a crisis. Treat it as a mirror.
One day a month, it shows you who actually runs your house.
She isn't the help.
She's the reason your marriage looks equal.

5496562a8394e733a9852288c37f1db43275f1b9.broken_premise: Premise 2 misdescribes the survey. The Time Use Survey records how much time each person in the sample actually spent on unpaid domestic work for their own household. The women it surveyed include those in households that already pay a domestic worker. So the roughly five hours (289 minutes in 2024) are the hours women still put in after any paid help, not hours a salary buys back. A worker who comes from 8 to 11 covers about three hours of tasks, while the survey's five hours are still being done by women. Two further limits: the figures cover all of India, not just urban homes, and they are averages over women who did housework that day. Premise 1 is the writer's generalization about everyday life, and paid part-time help is common in urban homes. Premise 3 is a description, not a claim about a market or law. Neither is falsifiable here. The headline gap the post uses (about 5 hours for women vs about 1.5 for men) is correct.
5496562a8394e733a9852288c37f1db43275f1b9.actual_mechanism: The survey measures each household member's own time. A paid domestic worker's hours aren't in the employer household's unpaid-work figures, and the hours the survey records are the work left after any help. A domestic worker therefore covers some of the chores, which would otherwise fall mostly on the wife. Even in households with help, women still do about 289 minutes a day of unpaid domestic work vs about 88 for men (2024, ages 6+). So paid help reduces the wife's load but doesn't bring it down to the husband's.
